lesson.title: Hot Air Rises, and So Does Its Volume: Charles's Law
lesson.summary: Charles's law states that at constant pressure and amount of gas, volume is directly proportional to absolute temperature, so heating a gas makes it expand and cooling it makes it contract.
lesson.body:
Charles's law is what remains of the ideal gas law when pressure and moles are held constant instead of temperature. Starting again from PV = nRT, if P, n, and R are all fixed, then rearranging gives V/T = nR/P, a constant. This means V/T stays the same before and after any change, which is usually written V1/T1 = V2/T2. Unlike Boyle's law, this is a direct relationship: as temperature increases, volume increases right along with it, and as temperature decreases, volume decreases too, as long as the pressure on the gas does not change.

The kinetic molecular theory again explains why. Raising the temperature of a gas increases the average kinetic energy, and therefore the average speed, of its particles. If the gas is allowed to expand while its pressure stays constant, meaning the container wall can move (think of a piston or a flexible balloon), the faster-moving particles push that wall outward until the collision frequency and force settle back down to match the fixed external pressure. The only way to keep pressure constant while particles are moving faster is for the volume to grow, spreading out the collisions over a larger area.

This is also exactly why temperature scales matter so much for gas law calculations. Charles's law only works correctly with an absolute temperature scale like Kelvin, because the relationship V1/T1 = V2/T2 assumes that V goes to zero as T goes to zero, which is only true if T is measured from absolute zero. Using Celsius directly would give nonsensical results, including negative or undefined volumes.

Here is a worked example. A gas sample occupies 2.00 L at 25 degrees Celsius, and you want to know its volume after heating it to 350 K at constant pressure. First, convert 25 degrees Celsius to Kelvin: 25 + 273 = 298 K. Then apply V1/T1 = V2/T2, rearranged to solve for V2: V2 = V1 times (T2 / T1) = 2.00 L times (350 K / 298 K). Multiplying first: 2.00 times 350 = 700. Dividing: 700 / 298 = 2.35 L. So the gas expands from 2.00 L to about 2.35 L, a roughly 17 percent increase in volume for a roughly 17 percent increase in absolute temperature (350/298 is about 1.17), which is exactly what a direct proportionality predicts.
